title: Remark on “Algorithm 778: L-BFGS-B: Fortran subroutines for large-scale bound constrained optimization”
contribution: A four-page revision of the 1997 L-BFGS-B code: the subspace step is projected onto the box and followed by backtracking (falling back to truncation when descent is not strong), and machine precision is taken from Fortran 90 EPSILON instead of the faulty dpmeps; tested old vs new on 38 large CUTEr problems (pp. 1-3).
problem_entry: Two defects in a released code: truncated subspace steps that make negligible progress on some problems, and dpmeps underestimating machine precision by two orders of magnitude on some Linux compilers (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Project the subspace minimizer onto l <= x <= u and backtrack along d_k = xbar_{k+1} - x_k, reverting to truncation if d_k is not a direction of strong descent; minimal exploration (cut-back and projection points only) keeps the phase cheap; EPSILON(x) replaces dpmeps (p. 2).
assumptions: Bound constraints only; 'strong descent' undefined; machine precision feeds a quasi-Newton safeguarding rule and a stop test; no theory (p. 2).
proof_devices: n/a: no theorem; projection justified by the literature on exploring the feasible boundary (Lin-More [5], GALAHAD [4]) and an unreported test of a more elaborate boundary search (p. 2)
experiments: 38 bound-constrained CUTEr/AMPL problems, n = 2,000-100,000, chosen large enough for reliable CPU timing; the old version given the correct machine precision so only the subspace change is measured; per-problem log2(FEVnew/FEVold) and log2(CPUnew/CPUold) plots with m = 20; verdict 'rather substantial' from the figures only (bars not recoverable from the text layer), no table, no dpmeps experiment, no other code (pp. 2-3).
positioning: Self-referential (1995 algorithm [1], 1997 code [6]); credits Lin-More and GALAHAD for boundary exploration and calls the gain 'not surprising' (pp. 2, 4).
writing: Three-sentence abstract stating both changes; four pages; unhedged verdict ('It is clear that the improvements in performance are rather substantial'); slips: keyword 'infeasibility', 'it it known' (pp. 1-3).
limits_future: No limitations or future directions written; unwritten limits: one 38-problem set, no theory, figure-only results, dpmeps cost not measured (pp. 2-3).

method_links.note: L-BFGS-B engine kept; only the subspace-step truncation replaced, with the old truncation kept as fallback when descent is not strong.
machine-precision estimate driving a safeguard and a stop test was wrong by two orders of magnitude and caused severe deterioration; repaired by a reliable source (EPSILON), not by a recovery path.

accounting corrected in the old version's favour (correct machine precision); CPU reported only where timing is reliable, evaluations too. Also full-text evidence for Heuristic 7 (published correction of the 1997 code) and Heuristic 5 (minimal two-point exploration kept as cheapest adequate option).
no losses discussed in the text, only the overall area of the per-problem plots.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the refinement of L-BFGS-B's subspace minimization phase is tied to faster identification of the optimal active set; same shape in S043 and S064

transferable: Port the bug fix into the old version before an old-vs-new comparison so the plot measures one change (p. 2).
Per-problem log2 ratios of function evaluations and CPU time, on problems large enough for reliable timing (pp. 2-3).
Projected subspace step with backtracking and automatic fallback to the truncated step when descent is not strong (p. 2).
Take machine precision from a language intrinsic when safeguards and stop tests depend on it (p. 2).

quotes.text: Our technique performs a minimal exploration (it only considers the cut-back and projection points) so as to keep the cost of the subspace minimization phase to a minimum.
This caused severe deterioration of performance on some problems because two important components of the algorithm rely on machine precision.

title: Newton-like methods for sparse inverse covariance estimation
contribution: Two classes of second-order methods for l1-penalized inverse covariance estimation, Newton-LASSO (piecewise quadratic model solved by FISTA) and orthant-based Newton (smooth quadratic on an orthant face by truncated CG), plus an L-BFGS variant, all exploiting the Kronecker Hessian structure; compared with a faithful MATLAB QUIC, C:QUIC and ALM on six synthetic problems, where no method dominates and OBN-LBFGS is proposed as the universal choice (pp. 2-8).
problem_entry: Covariance selection recast as min -log det P + trace(SP) + lambda ||vec P||_1; entry via the rival code QUIC, reported 'significantly faster' than five methods, whose coordinate-descent subproblem solver is questioned (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Free/active sets from the steepest-descent (min-norm subgradient) direction; NL minimizes the piecewise model (FISTA inner solver), OBN minimizes a smooth quadratic on the orthant face by K = O(1) CG steps using (A kron B)vec(C) = vec(BCA^T) at O(n^3); compact L-BFGS (from L-BFGS-B [24]) for the reduced minimizer; start at P0 = (diag(S) + lambda I)^-1 (pp. 2-6).
assumptions: Fixed lambda, i.i.d. samples, known mean, convex problem with unique P*; FISTA constant c > 1/(eigmin P_k)^2; no convergence theory (exact NL credited to Tseng-Yun; inexact NL and OBN deferred) (pp. 1-5).
proof_devices: n/a: no theorem; active/free sets derived from the steepest-descent direction so that a small step decreases the model (pp. 2-3)
Kronecker identity for O(n^3) reduced Hessian-vector products (22) (p. 6)
compact L-BFGS formula (24) for the reduced minimizer with operation count 2t^2|F| + 4t|F| (p. 6)
closed-form diagonal solution for lambda >= |S_ij| used as starting point (16) (p. 3)
inner-solver cost comparison O(Kn^3) FISTA vs O(Kn|F|) coordinate descent vs O(K_CG n^3) CG (p. 7)
assertion without argument that the OWL convergence proof is not correct (p. 4)
experiments: Six synthetic problems (n = 500, 1000, 2000; card(Sigma^-1) 1-20.1%; lambda = 0.5-0.01; card(P*), cond(P*) printed) with seven algorithms incl. a faithful MATLAB QUIC (NL-Coord), C:QUIC and ALM with its stopping test aligned; stop at 10n iterations or ||grad F||_inf <= 1e-6, 5000 s limit; iterations and seconds; no method dominates, NL-Coord best below 1% sparsity, C:QUIC best in the two sparsest settings, OBN-LBFGS the only finisher on one problem and called the universal choice; one cell exceeds the time limit without comment (pp. 6-8).
positioning: Surveys first- and second-order methods, takes QUIC as baseline on its own report, criticises OWL directly (reduced inverse Hessian 'difficult to justify', proof 'not correct'), credits Tseng-Yun and Dahl et al. (pp. 2-4, 6).
writing: Modest contribution sentence ('useful tools'); hedged results ('seem', 'appears'); untested expectations about optimized C codes; scope stated as methods and ideas rather than implementation efficiency; label slips ('OBN-Coord', 'OBM') (pp. 2, 4, 7).
limits_future: Convergence of inexact NL and of OBN deferred; QN inside Newton-LASSO omitted for brevity; MATLAB vs C gap; crude dynamic CG rule to be improved; unstated: synthetic data only, six problems (pp. 3-4, 6-8).

title: A family of second-order methods for convex ℓ1-regularized optimization
contribution: A semi-smooth Newton framework whose parameters (tau, delta) generate second-order ISTA, orthant-based and block active-set methods for f + mu||x||_1, plus a corrected block active-set method that checks and undoes mispredicted sign changes, with a nonzero-step theorem, a descent corollary, a noncycling safeguard and tests (130 BAS failures vs 0 on 1000 QPs; Newton-CBAS vs OWL-QN on one dataset) (2012 preprint, pp. 2-19).
problem_entry: Second-order methods for l1-regularized convex problems motivated by ML; the concrete entry is the known failure of BAS when Q is not an M-matrix, observed commonly as cycling (pp. 1-2, 10).
key_idea: Write optimality as a semi-smooth equation with free scale tau and generalized-Jacobian choice delta so that known methods are parameter settings; keep BAS's aggressive multi-change step but re-solve after moving mispredicted zero variables to the active set, until all predictions hold; safeguard by cardinality-based one-change backup; extend to general convex f by Newton-CBAS with Armijo backtracking (pp. 3-6, 10-11, 15, 18).
assumptions: f smooth convex, mu > 0 fixed; new algorithm designed for quadratic f with Q symmetric positive definite (Theorem 4.1); BAS efficient for M-matrices, fails otherwise; matching initialization (3.12) and complementary initial u, v (8.7) for the equivalence arguments (pp. 1-2, 7, 9-12, 21).
proof_devices: equivalence of semi-smooth Newton with BAS by induction on iterate and index-set relation (3.12) with case analysis (pp. 9-10)

Theorem 4.1: transition partition R, S, T, W (4.4) and sign vector (4.5); strict convexity of the reduced QP (4.9) gives a strict descent sum on T, corrected indices contribute nonnegative terms (pp. 12-13)
Corollary 4.2: directional derivative (4.12) split into zero, negative and nonpositive contributions, so d is a descent direction (pp. 13-14)
finiteness of the repeat loop because sets shrink each round (p. 11)
appendix: u - v split, KKT (8.3)-(8.6), y + z = 2 mu e, complementarity preserved, P<->N transitions impossible, reduction to a single vector (pp. 21-24)
Newton-CBAS descent via D phi(x; d) = D m(0; d) <= m(d) - m(0) < 0 by convexity (p. 18)
no rate and no global convergence proof for Algorithm 4.1; Algorithm 4.2 relies on the borrowed Judice-Pires safeguard (p. 15)
experiments: MATLAB framework with tau, delta as inputs; 1000 random QPs (sprandsym 25% density, condition ~1e4 or ~1e7, mu in [2.5, n/3], n not stated): BAS 10/500 + 120/500 failures (cycling) vs Corrected BAS 0, with 0.92-1.41 corrections per iteration; backup of Algorithm 4.2 (t_max = 10) never invoked; CPU performance profiles show OBM-COR somewhat more efficient and robustness costing extra computation; Newton-CBAS vs OWL-QN (same L-BFGS, memory 5) on StatLog Landsat, n = 7776, iterations only (pp. 17-19).
positioning: Inside semi-smooth Newton methodology; credits Hintermuller-Ito-Kunisch for the BAS-as-semi-smooth-Newton derivation and offers a different one; BAS lineage (Aganagic, Judice-Pires, Kim-Park) and Ben Gharbia-Gilbert nonconvergence cited; rivals (OWL-QN, QUIC, own reports) recast as special cases rather than criticised (pp. 2, 4-7, 9-10).
writing: 'two-fold' contribution sentence; interpretation of index sets as predictions before the algorithm; light hedging ('possibly due to'); rarity claims backed by one count; several typos (pp. 2, 10, 15-19).
limits_future: Algorithm 4.1 not globally convergent and may cycle; robustness costs computation; designed for quadratic f; only a few framework methods explored, second-order ISTA untested. Future: selective corrections, inexact steps, factorization updates, a descent-based safeguard, correction in second-order ISTA (pp. 2, 15-19).
